budgets.name: App + catalogue chunk, gzipped
budgets.why: What a first-time visitor actually downloads over the wire before the week screen is usable. The food catalogue and the recipe generator live in here on purpose — matching a spoken sentence, scanning a barcode and generating a plan all need the whole book, offline, immediately — so this is the number that stops the catalogue growing in silence. Raised Oct 2026 (300000 → 310000): the unified Home decision stack and leftover/waste evidence lines are deliberate first-paint product code, not catalogue growth — the catalogue-source budget below is unchanged and still caps the data itself. Raised again 27 Oct 2026 (310000 → 315000; uncompressed 960000 → 970000) for the Check before you shop card. Revisit by code-splitting the decision stack if this moves again.

budgets.name: App + catalogue chunk, uncompressed
budgets.why: The parse cost a phone pays before the app runs. Gzip hides it, so it is budgeted separately. Raised Oct 2026 (920000 → 960000) for the same deliberate first-paint product code as the gzip budget; still bites on any further growth.

budgets.name: Largest single JS chunk
budgets.why: One oversized chunk is a single unbreakable download. If this passes while the app chunk fails, a screen that can never load first has appeared. Raised Oct 2026 (800000 → 810000) alongside the app-chunk budgets for the same reason; still bites within ~1%.

budgets.name: All browser assets
budgets.why: Everything that ships to the browser, lazily loaded chunks included. A coarse ceiling on purpose, so a runaway dependency is caught even when it hides behind a dynamic import.

budgets.name: Catalogue data shipped eagerly
budgets.why: src/data is what the browser parses before anything can run — the single biggest thing in the bundle. It has to be measured, not assumed.

budgets.name: Client JS chunk count
budgets.why: A rising chunk count means fragments nobody loads and nobody caches well. Past this, split less, not more.
